payload.acceptance_criteria: every fixture that clears the ledger to install a known one clears both globs, asserted by the board corpus tests passing while a stray shard is still present rather than after it is removed
payload.description:
When a fixture replaces the ledger to pin a known corpus, I want it to clear the shards too, so I can stop a stray pending file inflating a frozen count.

Four fixtures cleared events-*.jsonl and not pending-*.jsonl, so a shard that happened to be tracked came along through work_repo and the board counted 7 records against a frozen 6. The pre-push gate caught it after the tag was cut locally.

This is the same sweep miss as basicly-zsq6xkz one layer out. That one found three readers that spelled the glob as a string literal rather than reading the kit constant; this one is the same literal in test fixtures, which the earlier sweep of log_paths callers could not see because a fixture is a writer and not a reader.

The stray shard itself was live data: five events the trunk did not hold, left uncompacted because the tutorial was dirty when the ledger was committed, so commit_tracker_state declined and the shard was committed raw.
payload.requirements: each site is edited by hand against a named count and reconciled after, because a scripted replace across test files is how 23 failures became 80 once before
payload.title: clear both ledger globs wherever a fixture installs a known ledger

payload.acceptance_criteria: ledger_git_rules returns the shard glob as well as the trunk glob, basicly install writes both into .gitattributes, and git check-attr reports merge union on a pending file in a repository installed through the engine, against the trunk file as the positive control
payload.description:
When a repository upgrades through basicly install rather than the standalone kit, I want its .gitattributes to carry the shard rule too, so I can stop two clones on one branch conflicting on a file the design exists to keep conflict-free.

Found by the terminal canary reading source at the v0.14.0 tag, filed there as term-n3rzn, and confirmed here. owned_write.ledger_git_rules returns only the events glob, and cli._scaffold_ledger_attributes appends exactly what it returns. The standalone installer writes both globs and docs/reference/kits.md promises both, so the two install paths diverge and the documentation describes the path a bundled consumer does not use.

This repository carries the rule only because it was hand-edited into .gitattributes during the sharding work, which is why no gate here noticed. A consumer installing v0.14.0 through the engine gets the trunk rule and not the shard rule.

The canary also corrected the framing and it matters. The shard name derives from .git/HEAD, so identity is per BRANCH, not per person. Two clones both sitting on main produce the same tracked path, and the GitHub measurement behind the release covers two different branches rather than that case. The repository's own test_two_writers_on_one_shard_still_need_the_union_attribute already proves union is load-bearing there, and the engine install is the path that lacks it.
payload.requirements: the engine reads both globs off the kit constants rather than spelling either a second time, because a second spelling is what left three readers blind in basicly-zsq6xkz. The wording that reads as one file per person is corrected wherever it appears.
payload.title: the engine install omits the shard merge rule the kit installer writes

payload.acceptance_criteria: the re-pin path writes the previous copy to the same .basicly-bak sibling the force path uses before it writes, and says where it is; a run that re-pins nothing writes no backup and leaves the file untouched
payload.description:
When an upgrade re-pins a consumer's CI workflow, I want the previous copy left beside it, so I can see what changed on a file my own rules put on a confirmation list.

Found by the terminal canary and filed there as term-42xuc arm 2. _write_scaffold at cli.py:1219-1241 inverts the safety: the plain path re-pins and writes in place with no backup, while the --overwrite-scaffolds branch writes a .basicly-bak sibling before replacing. So the flag that sounds destructive preserves the original and the default does not.

It is not theoretical for the canary. That repository carries the workflow with five pinned references and holds CI edits on an explicit confirmation list, so an upgrade rewrites a gated file before a human could be asked, and there is no install --dry-run to preview it.

Arm 1 of term-42xuc - a plain install CREATING a workflow where none existed, at the fallthrough that never consults force - is a larger question about what install may do unasked and is filed separately rather than rushed into this patch.
payload.requirements: one branch in _write_scaffold, no new flag and no change to what the force path does. The message names the backup by the same shape the force path already prints, so a consumer meets one vocabulary.
payload.title: back up a scaffold before the default path rewrites it

payload.acceptance_criteria: a decision is recorded naming whether creation stays default, becomes opt-in, or becomes announce-then-write, with the reason; whichever is chosen is enforced by a test that fails if install creates a workflow the chosen rule forbids
payload.description:
When an upgrade runs in a repository that has no CI workflow, I want to know whether creating one is something install may do without being asked, so I can stop a tool writing into a directory a consumer never opted into.

Found by the terminal canary as term-42xuc arm 1, confirmed here at cli.py:1239-1241: the branch that runs when the path does not exist calls mkdir and write and prints Wrote, and it never consults force. So --overwrite-scaffolds is not what arms creation; a plain install is. I reproduced it by accident in this repository, which had never tracked .github/workflows/basicly-gates.yml and had one after a mistaken install.

Re-pinning a file a consumer already has is a different act from creating one they never had, and the second is the larger one. This is filed apart from basicly-kfj94k8, which only removes the backup inversion, because the answer here is a decision rather than a defect.

The canary listed four shapes without prescribing one: announce before writing, back up on the re-pin path, gate creation behind an explicit opt-in, or add install --dry-run. The second is done. The remaining three are alternatives, not a sequence.
payload.requirements: the decision is written where the other fifty are rather than in a changelog entry. No behaviour changes until it is taken, because the current behaviour is documented in the file's own first line and changing it silently is the same class of surprise being complained about.
payload.title: decide whether a plain install may create a ci workflow unasked
